idiom_name: PORO domain objects + repository over an ActiveRecord (or Sequel/ROM) data model
implementation_notes: Ruby gives you the pieces but not the structure: domain objects are plain classes, Data or Struct instances (with constructor validation and freeze for value objects), and the mapping is written by hand in a repository that turns ActiveRecord/Sequel rows or ROM relations into those objects (to_domain) and back (to_record). What replaces the classic Mapper is that repository pair of methods plus, for reads, query objects; ROM (ROM::Struct, relations, changesets, repositories) can supply the whole structure as a library if the project accepts its functional style and no lazy loading. ActiveRecord must be treated as the data model only - inheriting from ActiveRecord::Base puts persistence, typecasting, callbacks and validations into the same class that is supposed to own the invariants.
pitfalls: Rails conventions pull the model back into ActiveRecord: callbacks, scopes, validations and typecasting live on the AR class, so 'the model' silently becomes the table again unless the AR classes are named and treated as records (OrderRecord).
method_missing-based attribute access hides shape drift: a renamed or missing column yields nil at mapping time instead of an error.

ROM and other data-mapper toolkits remove lazy loading and self-saving: everything must be loaded through repositories explicitly, which is a design change, not just a library swap, and it adds boilerplate for simple CRUD.
